source.title_on_document: Writing, creativity, and artificial intelligence. ChatGPT in the university context

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplementary material. All statistics are in Tables 2 to 5 of the main text.

paper_design_summary: Two designs. First, 20 free or freemium text-generation AI systems and 193 Spanish university students each completed Games 2 (uses of a rubber tube) and 3 (what if people never stopped growing) of the Spanish PIC-A creative imagination test, and the paper compares AI and student scores on fluency, flexibility, and narrative originality with Mann-Whitney U tests. Second, in a non-randomized pretest-posttest design, the same students first played both games without aid and then repeated them with ChatGPT, instructed to improve their earlier answers, and the paper compares pretest and posttest scores with Wilcoxon tests.

studies.label: AI systems versus students on PIC-A Games 2 and 3 (descriptive, ex post facto comparison)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. Scores of 20 AI systems are compared with the unaided (pretest) scores of 193 students.
assignment.quote: a descriptive and comparative non-experimental or ex post-facto quantitative research study was carried out, in which the level of creativity achieved by both the AI systems and the students was analysed

arms.name: AI systems

participants.who: Undergraduate and master's students in Primary Education, Early Childhood and Primary Education research, Fine Arts, and Audio-visual Communication and Journalism; 153 women and 40 men aged 18 to 50; non-probabilistic convenience sample
participants.country: Spain (University of Murcia, University of Salamanca, Miguel Hernández University of Elche)

ai_tool.name_model: 20 LLM text-generation systems, all 'with OpenAI/GPT-3 technology (except Dupla.ai, a Chrome extension)' (Table 1)
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers typed each PIC-A game instruction into each system three times in a row and collected the responses, which were then scored with the PIC-A correction notebook. The games were run as the first action after accessing each system.

task.description: PIC-A (Creative Imagination Test for Adults, Artola et al. 2012) Game 2: list uses of a rubber tube (alternate uses). Game 3: imagine what would happen if people never stopped growing (consequences).
task.duration: Students: 10 minutes per game per the manual. AI: no time limit; three successive requests per instruction.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: S1 and S2 use the same 193 students; the S1 human scores equal the S2 pretest scores (Table 4 vs Table 5). No overlap with another paper is stated.
sample_overlap.quote: The students repeated the games, assisted by ChatGPT, to compare the possible improvement of their productions.
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 1 (journal p. 45), Abstract; PDF p. 7, Tables 4 and 5

company_involvement.description: Funded by a Spanish R&D&I project (PID2020-113731GB-I00, MCIN/AEI); no AI company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: No random assignment. S1 compares 20 AI systems' output with students' unaided output (ai_vs_human context). S2 is a one-group pretest-posttest in which all 193 students did the unaided pretest first and the ChatGPT posttest second, with the instruction to improve their earlier answers (quasi_people, which the codebook folds into observational). Outcomes are scored on the output (PIC-A fluency, flexibility, narrative originality) and the sample is 193 people, but criterion 1 fails.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT, students' Game 2 scores rose from pretest to posttest (fluency 10.47 to 13.08, flexibility 7.56 to 8.33, narrative originality 11.02 to 14.45, all p <= .002), Game 3 fluency rose slightly (9.52 to 10.05, p = .025), and AI systems outscored students on Game 2 but not Game 3 (PDF p. 7, Tables 4 and 5).
open_questions: Whether a one-group pretest-posttest (quasi_people) design enters the site as observational context or only in the screening report (codebook Section 13).
The paper does not state the n per comparison in Tables 4 and 5 or whether any of the 193 students missed the posttest.

For the 20 AI systems, each instruction was sent three times; the paper does not say whether the three responses were pooled, averaged, or one chosen, so the AI-side unit (system vs response) is unclear.
The posttest confounds AI help with a second attempt at the same items (practice and revision of the pretest text); there is no unaided second-attempt comparison group.
notes: Tables use decimal commas. Table 5 Z statistics carry superscript b with no footnote printed. Table 3 also reports student descriptives by gender (men/women), not coded as a contrast. S1 outcome unit is coded 'output': one scored response set per AI system (20) or per student (193) for each game. Effect sizes in Tables 4 and 5 are labeled only 'Effect size' (the paper calls .4 values 'moderate' and lower values 'low'); the formula is not stated. Measure 'category_count' is used for all three PIC-A indicators because they are computed from answer counts and category frequency coefficients in the manual; the paper does not name the scorers for student answers.
